tagline.text: Bulacan's May 14 thanksgiving festival, when carabaos kneel before the church

location.label: Location
location.text: In front of San Isidro Labrador Parish Church and the streets of Pulilan, Bulacan

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Every May 14 (the day before the May 15 feast of San Isidro)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: Public street parade. Budget for transport, meals and any lodging separately

children.text: Pulilan’s Carabao Festival in Bulacan centers on the May 14 buffalo parade and the May 15 feast of San Isidro Labrador. Decorated buffalo pass through town and kneel in front of the parish church on May 14.
The
Pulilan municipal guide

places the annual buffalo parade at 2 p.m. on May 14. May 15 is the feast of San Isidro Labrador, patron saint of farmers. Check that year’s notice for the start location, road closures and start time.

The parade is the heart of the event. Farmers from Pulilan's 19 barangays, nearby Bulacan municipalities and Nueva Ecija, among other places, bring their carabaos and march through the town streets. The carabaos are decorated with paint, garlands and ornaments, and at the climax of the parade trained carabaos kneel in front of San Isidro Labrador Parish Church to show reverence. Floats from each barangay, student street dancers and marching bands join the procession as well.

The number of participating carabaos is reported differently from year to year. A 2015 report said up to 800 carabaos take part, and a 2016 report said more than 700 took part. Another report from the same year said only about 100 of roughly 500 carabaos knelt, so keep in mind that not every carabao kneels. A report also said about 100,000 people gathered in 2023, after the COVID restrictions ended.

As for the origin, some accounts describe an old custom that began in Spanish colonial times, using San Isidro to draw people to Catholicism, while other sources say the kneeling carabao event itself was created relatively recently. Either way, it has become Pulilan's signature event, tied to the feast of San Isidro. The schedule and details change from year to year, so check the latest announcements from Pulilan's municipal government. There is also some local context that helps you understand the festival. According to a 2015 report, the municipal government gave ₱1,000 per participating carabao instead of gift packs, and there was no limit on how many carabaos one family could bring, so some families brought three or more. Participants pray together for the health of their carabaos and the peace of their town. In other words, it is first a village celebration in which farmers close out the farming year, and only then something tourists come to watch, so please watch respectfully.

When the parade reaches San Isidro Labrador Parish Church, trained carabaos kneel. It is a ritual in which farmers give thanks to the saint, and also a chance to show how well the carabaos are trained. A 2016 report said about 100 carabaos knelt, so keep in mind that only some carabaos do this.

Hundreds of carabaos, decorated with paint and garlands, march through the town streets. Farmers pray for the health of their carabaos and the peace of their town. Some farmers from neighboring towns have joined for decades, which gives the event a sense of long tradition.

Each of Pulilan's 19 barangays decorates a float with the crops it is known for. One report said about 10 floats came from commercial businesses. It is fun to compare what each village takes pride in.

blocks.title: San Isidro Labrador Parish Church and museum

children.text: The church, where the parade ends, is a 19th-century Baroque church in the poblacion (town center), and there is said to be a San Isidro Labrador museum on the same grounds. The plaza in front of the church is the main stage for the parade and the kneeling.
The
municipal festival guide

distinguishes the May 14 buffalo parade from the May 15 street dancing. Proclamation No. 1213 made May 14, 2026 a special non-working day in Pulilan. Check the latest program for the next festival’s event times and venues.

During the festival you can reportedly talk with farmers and learn about sustainable farming and how carabaos are used. For visitors from the city, it is a rare chance to see Philippine rural culture up close.

blocks.title: The story of San Isidro Labrador

children.text: San Isidro is said to have been born in 1070 to a poor family in Madrid, Spain, worked for a wealthy landowner, and died on May 15, 1120. He was believed to have brought bountiful crops through his kindness to the poor and to animals, and he was canonized in 1622. Locally he is affectionately called Tata Sidro.
Leave Metro Manila. Roads in downtown Pulilan are closed on festival day, so arrive early and find a spot along the parade route.
Arrive in Pulilan's poblacion and look around the church area. Parade times differ each year, so check municipal announcements.
Visit the parish church and town before the buffalo parade. Check the viewing area and barriers outside the church.
Have lunch at a restaurant or street stall in town. It is crowded on festival day, so eating early is easier.
Watch the afternoon buffalo parade listed by the municipality, then leave once crowds ease. Keep a safe distance from the animals.
This example uses the municipal guide’s 2 p.m. departure. Check the actual parade time and road closures for that year.
Visit Malolos Cathedral and Barasoain Church in the morning.

items.title: Arrive-the-day-before plan
items.subtitle: An unhurried two days, one night

children.text: Arrive in Pulilan or nearby Malolos on the afternoon before the festival and leave your bags at your lodging.
Walk around the church in the poblacion and scout the road the parade will take and the plaza in front of the church.
Have dinner at a restaurant in town and rest early. Shops may close early the night before an event, so check locally.
Early the next morning, go out around the church and watch the farmers and their decorated carabaos.
Watch the parade and kneeling ceremony according to the municipal schedule, then head home.
The arrive-the-day-before plan is a sample itinerary put together for this research. Check lodging and transport locally.

items.title: Bus and UV Express from Manila

children.text: Pulilan is about
43 km

northwest of Manila (the town's own figure; the straight-line distance is about 37 km). Buses and UV Express vans reportedly run to Pulilan from Grace Park, Divisoria, Monumento and Cubao in Metro Manila. You get on and off at Pulilan Junction and the SM Center Pulilan terminal.
NLEX is Pulilan's only expressway, with exits in Barangays Dampol 2nd A and Tibag.
Access to town may be blocked on festival day, so check fares and times locally.
From the NLEX exit, the road connects to the Pulilan Regional Road (N115). Traffic is controlled around the poblacion on festival day, so plan to park on the outskirts and walk.
You can also take a taxi from Metro Manila.
Jeepneys and tricycles are the basic way to get around Pulilan. Jeepneys run from the Robinsons Townville terminal along the Pulilan Regional Road (N115) and to nearby barangays.
Around the church, walking is the fastest way to get around.

To see the Carabao Festival, you need to go on May 14. May is when the hottest part of the Philippine year ends and the rainy season begins, so daytime temperatures are high and showers are possible. The parade takes place outdoors in the middle of the day, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
On days without the festival, Pulilan is a quiet town. You can visit the church and museum, but check opening hours locally.

The parade takes place in the daytime when crowds are largest, and one report said about 100,000 people gathered in 2023, so it is best to arrive early and claim a spot. If you are making a day trip from Manila, buses back all fill at once after the parade, so either delay your return or line up early at the terminal.

Pulilan is close enough to Manila for a day trip, so not many people stay overnight. If you stay, you can look for lodging in nearby Malolos or in Pulilan town, but we did not confirm any specific place in this research, so check recent reviews on booking sites. Rooms fill up quickly the night before and on the day of the festival.

In town you can find Filipino soups, grilled dishes and snacks at restaurants and street stalls. Lines get long on festival day, so eat early and bring plenty of water. As for establishments, it is best to go only to places you have confirmed are still open.
If you want to see carabaos up close, go before the parade starts, when farmers are decorating them. When taking photos, it is polite to ask the farmer first. Giving a small thank-you is up to you.
The parade follows the town's streets. Arrive early in the morning and take a spot near the front of the church.
Avoid sudden movements near the carabaos and keep a safe distance. Loud noises or flash can startle them.
The midday sun is strong, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
If you go from Manila by public transport, allow plenty of time for the return trip. The terminals are crowded after the festival.
Keep your belongings in a front bag and watch for pickpockets in crowds.
Dress modestly when entering the church grounds.
The parade timetable changes every year, so check the latest announcements from Pulilan's municipal government.
On festival day the roads in Pulilan's poblacion are closed and crowds make it hard to move. Carabaos are large animals, so do not approach them closely without a rope.
Do not stand near the carabaos' path or close to the road.
The number of participating carabaos and kneeling carabaos varies from year to year. Not every carabao kneels.
The schedule and program (street dancing, performances, fair) change every year and are sometimes canceled. For example, a carabao race was canceled in 2016.
Mid-May is very hot. Watch out for heatstroke and drink water often.
Book transport and lodging for festival day early, or leave some slack in your schedule.
